analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off the coasts of California, Oregon, and Washington.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently ban West Coast offshore drilling never got a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee from February 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from ever issuing a lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in federal waters off California, Oregon, or Washington. Because it is written as a statutory ban that overrides other laws, it could not be undone by a future administration's drilling plan. It was never brought up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities and the people who depend on the ocean economy — commercial and recreational fishing, tourism, and beach towns — would gain permanent protection from the risk of an offshore oil spill along the West Coast. Ordinary taxpayers would avoid bearing the cleanup and economic costs of a spill, which historically far exceed what companies pay. The ban would also keep a publicly owned resource off the table for an industry that currently leases those waters at low cost relative to the public risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, fishing and tourism economies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management from issuing any lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in the outer Continental Shelf off California, Oregon, or Washington.

Makes the ban permanent and shields it from reversal: the amendment says it applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of this section or any other law,' so a future administration could not open West Coast waters through a new five-year leasing plan.

By closing the door on new leasing, the bill would remove the possibility of offshore drilling infrastructure — platforms, pipelines, and tankers — being placed along a coastline whose fisheries and tourism economies would absorb the damage of any spill.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would permanently lose access to potential new drilling areas off the West Coast. The federal Treasury would forgo whatever lease bonuses, rents, and royalties future sales in those waters might have generated, and consumers would forgo a marginal amount of domestic energy supply — though there is no active West Coast offshore drilling program today, so the cost is largely prospective rather than immediate.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently locks away offshore oil and gas resources off three states, forgoing potential federal lease revenue and domestic production. Supporters of expanded drilling argue domestic production supports energy supply and energy security, and a permanent statutory ban eliminates any flexibility to revisit that tradeoff in a national emergency.

The ban would cost some potential high-paying energy jobs in the region, though West Coast waters currently have no active new leasing program, so the immediate economic loss is small compared with the avoided spill risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but precautionary: West Coast federal waters are not being drilled today, so the bill's main value is preventing future administrations from opening them, which is exactly what the administration proposed at the time. The cost — forgone potential lease revenue and some future production — is borne by the oil industry and the Treasury, not by ordinary people directly. On balance a modest, low-cost protection for coastal economies that, because it never came to a vote, delivered nothing in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee a month later, and never moved again before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on January 8, 2019, with 17 original cosponsors, in response to the Trump administration's push to expand offshore drilling into new waters.
The House referred it to the Natural Resources Committee, the committee with jurisdiction over offshore energy, where it sat.

On February 5, 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources — the last action ever taken; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests and any administration that wants the option to lease West Coast waters came out ahead: no permanent ban was enacted, so West Coast drilling remains a decision for whoever holds the White House and Interior rather than a settled matter of law.

for.name: Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 original cosponsors on day one.

for.name: 32 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat, all from or aligned with West Coast districts.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Raúl Grijalva, D)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee on February 5, 2019 and never advanced it — no hearing, markup, or vote in the two years that followed.

against.name: Trump administration
against.what_they_did: Proposed expanding offshore drilling to new areas, which was the impetus for the bill; the administration opposed statutory bans on new offshore leasing.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Democratic-led committee also declined to move the bill, so it never reached a floor vote where party lines could be tested.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar them from ever leasing West Coast federal waters for exploration, development, or production. Their financial interest in opening those waters runs directly against the coastal economies that would bear the cost of a spill.
A spill or drilling infrastructure off the West Coast would hit commercial fisheries, recreation, and beach tourism first. The ban protects the coastline those industries and their customers rely on.
